exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Malina, where the unnamed narrator lives with two men, one real and one invented. Notice how Bachmann blurs dream and waking. Write how the novel makes a woman's interiority the battleground of history.

name: Hans Fallada
teaser: The German novelist of everyday resistance. Alone in Berlin follows an ordinary couple scattering postcards against the Nazis — a small, doomed, magnificent act of defiance. Also wrote the grim Little Man, What Now?

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Alone in Berlin. Notice how Fallada builds suspense out of the smallest risks — a card dropped on a stairwell. Write how the Quangels' quiet rebellion grows in weight and danger.

name: Uwe Johnson
teaser: The German novelist who grew up on the East-West border and made division his subject. Speculations About Jakob and Anniversaries track characters shuttling between two Germanys, two loyalties, two selves.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Anniversaries, dated diary entries from New York that keep circling back to 1960s Germany. Notice how Johnson's narrator observes America with a refugee's double vision. Write what the two countries mirror in each other.

name: Ernst Jünger
teaser: The German soldier-writer whose Storm of Steel made trench warfare a kind of terrible adventure. Later he turned inward, writing On the Marble Cliffs against tyranny and keeping a vast, aphoristic war diary.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Storm of Steel. Notice how Jünger describes combat with intense, almost aesthetic concentration, without judgment. Write how this cool witness of war both fascinates and unsettles a modern reader.

name: Siegfried Lenz
teaser: The German novelist of northern sea and moral choice. The German Lesson follows a boy assigned to police a painter's prohibition — a fable about duty, art, and the gray zones of obedience.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The German Lesson, set in a reformatory where the narrator writes the assigned essay that becomes the novel. Notice how Lenz frames the story as punishment and memory. Write how 'duty' becomes the story's tragic engine.

name: Johann Peter Hebel
teaser: The German-Alemannic writer whose calendar stories — tiny tales of cleverness, luck, and judgment — were admired by Kafka, Benjamin, and countless readers for their perfect economy and warmth.

exploreAction.targetName: The Treasure Chest stories, a selection
exploreAction.instruction: Read three short pieces from The Treasure Chest. Notice how each story is built to fit a calendar page, with a turn at the end. Write what makes a small story feel complete, and which of Hebel's tales you'd retell.

name: Ivan Turgenev
teaser: The most European of the great Russians — elegant, melancholic, precise. Fathers and Sons gave the word 'nihilist' to the world, and his Sportsman's Sketches helped end serfdom.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Fathers and Sons, where Bazarov arrives with his sleeves rolled up and his opinions ready. Notice how Turgenev stages the clash of generations without taking sides. Write what nihilism meant in 1862 and what it means now.

name: Nikolai Gogol
teaser: The Ukrainian-born Russian genius of the grotesque. Dead Souls, The Overcoat, and The Nose turned Russian bureaucracy into surreal comedy that still stings — and made every writer after him measure themselves against him.

exploreAction.instruction: Read The Overcoat. Notice how Akaky Akakievich's whole life narrows to one coat, then the story turns fantastical. Write how Gogol makes us laugh at a clerk and then grieve for him — and what the ghost at the end is really doing.

name: Alexander Pushkin
teaser: The founding poet of Russian literature, who died in a duel at 37. Eugene Onegin invented the Russian novel in verse, and his tales made the language sing. Everything Russian literary starts at his door.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Eugene Onegin. Notice how Pushkin's narrator keeps interrupting the story with asides, jokes, and footnotes. Write how the 'Onegin stanza' creates a chatty, intimate voice that made Russian poetry feel newly alive.

name: Mikhail Lermontov
teaser: The Romantic poet and novelist who died at 27 in a duel he chose. A Hero of Our Time gave literature its first 'superfluous man' — Pechorin, bored, brilliant, and dangerous to everyone he meets.

exploreAction.targetName: A Hero of Our Time, Bela
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first story, Bela. Notice how the novel arrives at Pechorin through other people's accounts before he speaks. Write how Lermontov builds the portrait of a man who ruins others partly out of boredom with himself.

name: Boris Pasternak
teaser: Russian poet and novelist of Doctor Zhivago — a love story across revolution and war that got him the Nobel he was forced to refuse. His poetry moves with the force of weather and history.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Doctor Zhivago, where the young Yuri sees his mother buried in a snow-covered field. Notice how Pasternak ties private grief to the coming storm of history. Write how the novel treats the individual against the collective.

name: Anna Akhmatova
teaser: Russia's great poet of witness and loss. Requiem, written in secret about the Stalinist terror, stands among the century's most harrowing poems — a mother's voice speaking for millions of silent women.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Requiem, where Akhmatova waits in prison lines with the other women. Notice how the personal and the national fuse. Write what it means to 'speak for' those who cannot, and what courage her spare lines carry.

name: Marina Tsvetaeva
teaser: The Russian poet of explosive, irregular genius — diction that breaks syntax to say what it must. She lived in exile and poverty, and her letters and poems burn with intensity that later poets still feed on.

exploreAction.instruction: Read three of Tsvetaeva's poems. Notice how her punctuation and line breaks create urgency. Write how her style differs from more 'finished' poets, and what kind of truth demands broken syntax.

name: Osip Mandelstam
teaser: The Russian poet of classical clarity and terrible courage — he died in the camps after writing a poem against Stalin. His poetry balances stone-hard precision with deep musicality.

exploreAction.instruction: Read three of Mandelstam's poems, including one from the Voronezh notebooks. Notice how images of stone, water, and breath recur. Write how a poet composes when every word is dangerous, and what clarity means under threat.

name: Andrei Platonov
teaser: The strangest of Russian modernists — a Soviet writer whose skewed, tender, bureaucratic prose revealed the human wreckage of utopia. The Foundation Pit and Chevengur are bleak and holy books.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Foundation Pit. Notice how Platonov's workers dig with devotion while the language goes slightly wrong, like a badly translated dream. Write how his broken official prose mocks and mourns the project at once.

name: Isaac Babel
teaser: The Odessa-born writer of Red Cavalry — short, brutal, lyrical stories set in the Polish campaign — and of the Jewish gangsters of Odessa. He wrote slowly, perfectly, and was executed in 1940.

exploreAction.targetName: Red Cavalry, a cluster of stories
exploreAction.instruction: Read three stories from Red Cavalry. Notice how Babel compresses violence and beauty into a page — a field, a corpse, a sunset. Write how a writer of Jewish Odessa rode with Cossacks and looked at them with both awe and grief.

name: Yevgeny Zamyatin
teaser: The Russian engineer who wrote We, the dystopia that taught Orwell and Huxley their blueprints — a glass city of numbers and scheduled happiness. He saw the totalitarian future coming and said so in 1924.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the first 'records' of We. Notice how the narrator writes in numbered diary entries and calls himself D-503. Write how the language of the state colonizes even private feeling, and why the story remains so prophetic.

name: Stanisław Lem
teaser: The Polish science-fiction philosopher. Solaris and His Master's Voice ask whether we can ever understand an alien mind — and our own. He made sci-fi a laboratory for epistemology and wit.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Solaris. Notice how Lem's ocean-planet resists interpretation, and how the scientists project their own guilt onto it. Write what the novel suggests about the limits of knowledge and the loneliness of contact.

name: Czesław Miłosz
teaser: The Polish poet of witness and exile, who lived through the Nazi occupation of Warsaw and later taught in California. His poetry asks how one speaks after catastrophe — and his Nobel speech became a moral landmark.

exploreAction.targetName: Miłosz, poems from the war years
exploreAction.instruction: Read poems like A Poor Christian Looks at the Ghetto and Campo dei Fiori. Notice how Miłosz keeps turning from the event to the question of who tells it. Write what it means for poetry to 'witness' without being consumed.

name: Ivan Goncharov
teaser: The Russian novelist who gave the world Oblomov — the man who cannot get out of bed. A comic masterpiece of inertia, and one of the sharpest portraits of a soul in retreat from life.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Oblomov, where the hero stays on his sofa through every visitor's appeal. Notice how Goncharov makes inaction hilarious and strangely moving. Write what Oblomov's refusal means — laziness, protest, or fear?

name: Varlam Shalamov
teaser: The Russian writer who survived seventeen years in the Kolyma labor camps and spent his life writing Kolyma Tales — short, unsparing stories that refuse all comfort and nearly all metaphor.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one story from Kolyma Tales. Notice how Shalamov reports the camps without sentiment — frostbite, bread, the logic of survival. Write why he said prose must be 'cold' and what that coldness preserves.

name: Mikhail Sholokhov
teaser: The Cossack novelist of And Quiet Flows the Don — an epic of revolution told through one family's river of blood and love. He won the Nobel and remains Russia's most monumental storyteller of the civil war.

exploreAction.targetName: And Quiet Flows the Don, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of the epic, where the river and the village are introduced through the Melekhov family. Notice how Sholokhov grounds vast history in one household. Write how the Don itself becomes a character.

name: Andrey Bely
teaser: The Russian symbolist whose novel Petersburg is a prose symphony of the city — a cubist, ticking, hallucinated Petersburg on the eve of revolution. Nabokov ranked it among the greatest novels of the century.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Petersburg. Notice how the city is described in fragments, rhythms, and strange geometries. Write how the prose itself performs the nervous energy of the revolution it narrates.

name: Sławomir Mrożek
teaser: The Polish playwright and cartoonist of the absurd. His short stories and dramas, like Tango, use surreal logic to expose totalitarian habits — funny, bleak, and devastatingly precise.

exploreAction.instruction: Read three of Mrożek's very short stories. Notice how each begins with a plausible situation that tilts into the absurd. Write how comedy becomes a way of telling the truth about power that plain description cannot reach.

name: Aleksandar Hemon
teaser: The Bosnian-American novelist stranded in Chicago by the siege of Sarajevo, who learned English and wrote The Question of Bruno and The Lazarus Project — memory, displacement, and history braided together.

exploreAction.targetName: The Question of Bruno, a story
exploreAction.instruction: Read a story from The Question of Bruno. Notice how Hemon scrambles chronology, genre, and voice. Write how the experience of exile shapes a writer's relationship to language — what does it mean to be 'born again' into English?

name: Andrey Kurkov
teaser: The Ukrainian novelist of the absurd and the everyday — Death and the Penguin follows a writer who keeps a penguin named Misha in post-Soviet Kyiv. His books read like black comedies of survival.

exploreAction.targetName: Death and the Penguin, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Death and the Penguin. Notice how Viktor's life — obituaries for the living, a penguin for company — is both surreal and perfectly believable. Write how the penguin becomes a mirror of its owner's isolation.

name: Serhiy Zhadan
teaser: The Ukrainian poet and novelist of the east — Kharkiv's chronicler. Voroshilovgrad and The Orphanage mix punk energy, tenderness, and war; his poetry speaks for a generation living through upheaval.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Orphanage. Notice how Zhadan balances the surreal violence of war with precise domestic detail. Write how the novel treats the duty to protect one child while the world burns around you.

name: Mikhail Saltykov-Shchedrin
teaser: The great Russian satirist of the 19th century, whose The Golovlyov Family and The History of a Town flayed bureaucracy, serfdom, and hypocrisy with savage laughter. Dostoevsky called him a prophet.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Golovlyov Family. Notice how Saltykov-Shchedrin's portrait of a decaying gentry family mixes farce and horror. Write how the novel's central figure, Iudushka, becomes a study in sanctimonious cruelty.

name: Henrik Ibsen
teaser: The Norwegian playwright who made the modern drama — A Doll's House, Hedda Gabler, and Ghosts ripped open the respectable home and let the 19th century's lies out. Every argument play owes him a debt.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the first act of A Doll's House. Notice how Nora performs her little-bird role while secretly managing a huge debt. Write how Ibsen plants the crisis in the first scene, and what the 'doll's house' metaphor contains.

name: Hans Christian Andersen
teaser: The Danish storyteller whose fairy tales — The Little Mermaid, The Ugly Duckling, The Snow Queen — are darker, stranger, and more honest than their Disney versions. He wrote about longing and being an outsider.

exploreAction.targetName: The Little Mermaid, the original tale
exploreAction.instruction: Read the original Little Mermaid. Notice how different it is from the cartoon — pain, sacrifice, and an ending about souls rather than weddings. Write what the tale really says about love, transformation, and loss.

name: Karen Blixen
teaser: The Danish baroness who wrote as Isak Dinesen — author of Out of Africa and Seven Gothic Tales. Her ornate, ironic, storytelling-rich prose made her one of the 20th century's most distinctive voices.

exploreAction.instruction: Read Babette's Feast. Notice how Blixen builds a whole theology of generosity around a French cook and a puritan village. Write what the dinner means as a work of art — and what the story says about giving everything.

name: Sigrid Undset
teaser: The Norwegian Nobel laureate whose medieval epic Kristin Lavransdatter follows one woman's fierce life across marriage, faith, and motherhood in 14th-century Norway. Few novels render a soul so completely.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Wreath. Notice how Undset immerses you in medieval Norwegian domestic life — food, cloth, weather — without costume-pageant decoration. Write how the historical setting deepens rather than decorates the love story.

name: Tarjei Vesaas
teaser: The Norwegian master of the spare, the elemental. The Ice Palace is a short novel about two girls and an ice formation that is one of the most haunting books ever written in any language.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Ice Palace. Notice how Vesaas writes in short, precise sentences that feel translated from snow and silence. Write how the frozen waterfall becomes both a real place and a state of feeling.

name: Karl Ove Knausgård
teaser: The Norwegian writer whose six-volume My Struggle became a literary event — a memoir-novel of radical honesty that turns washing dishes and remembering a father into gripping, ordinary revelation.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of My Struggle. Notice how Knausgård's attention to the mundane becomes hypnotic. Write what total candor costs and gives a writer — and why the smallest details can carry the largest grief.

name: Henning Mankell
teaser: The Swedish crime writer who made the police procedural literary. His Kurt Wallander novels map the underside of Swedish welfare society — melancholy, migration, and a detective who feels the cold of the world.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Faceless Killers. Notice how the crime arrives inside a landscape of isolation — snow, dawn, an empty farmhouse. Write how Mankell uses the mystery to ask what a society hides from itself.

name: Stieg Larsson
teaser: The Swedish journalist whose Millennium trilogy — The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and its sequels — became a global phenomenon. Lisbeth Salander is modern crime fiction's most iconic outsider.

exploreAction.targetName: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, prologue
exploreAction.instruction: Read the prologue, set in the 1960s. Notice how Larsson builds a cold, corporate world where power hides abuse. Write how the novel's twin heroes — journalist and hacker — approach the same corruption from opposite sides.

name: Fredrik Backman
teaser: The Swedish author of A Man Called Ove and Anxious People — warm, funny novels about grumpy people and the communities that insist on loving them. Best-sellers that smuggle in real grief.

exploreAction.targetName: A Man Called Ove, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of A Man Called Ove. Notice how Backman makes a rigid, complaining man immediately endearing. Write how comedy and tenderness share the same sentences, and what the novel says about grief and routine.

name: Pär Lagerkvist
teaser: The Swedish Nobel laureate who asked the big questions in small, stark books. Barabbas retells the crucifixion from the released murderer's bewildered point of view — faith as absence, doubt as presence.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Barabbas. Notice how Lagerkvist keeps the style bare and biblical. Write what it means to be the man who lived instead of Christ — how does the novel make doubt itself a form of searching?

name: Astrid Lindgren
teaser: The Swedish children's author who redefined childhood on the page — Pippi Longstocking, the Children of Noisy Village, and the fierce brothers of the Lionheart. She trusted children with grief and freedom.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Pippi Longstocking. Notice how Pippi breaks every rule of the polite village without malice. Write how Lindgren's anarchic heroine made room for children's power, imagination, and kindness on their own terms.

name: Tove Jansson
teaser: The Finnish-Swedish artist who created the Moomins — and wrote adult fiction of equal subtlety. Her Moominvalley books are philosophical comfort objects, and her later stories are sharp, quiet masterpieces.

exploreAction.instruction: Read a chapter of The Summer Book, about a grandmother and granddaughter on a Finnish island. Notice how Jansson renders the natural world with precise, unshowy detail. Write what the island teaches about attention and letting go.

name: Mika Waltari
teaser: The Finnish novelist of The Egyptian — one of the best-selling historical novels ever, a court physician's confession set in the Egypt of the pharaohs, full of immortality, plague, and human weakness.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Egyptian. Notice how Waltari frames the tale as a memoir written by a man who has lost everything. Write how the ancient setting lets him discuss timeless questions of ambition, love, and death.

name: Arto Paasilinna
teaser: The Finnish novelist of deadpan absurdity. The Year of the Hare follows a journalist who chucks it all to chase a hare across Finland — a comic ode to escape, wilderness, and saying no to everything.

exploreAction.targetName: The Year of the Hare, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Year of the Hare. Notice how Paasilinna keeps a straight face through increasingly surreal events. Write how the hare functions as a living excuse for freedom, and what the novel says about modern life.

name: Halldór Laxness
teaser: The Icelandic Nobel laureate who wrote Independent People — the story of Bjartur of Summerhouses, a sheep farmer who would rather starve than owe anyone, in one of the greatest novels about stubbornness.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Independent People. Notice how Laxness treats Bjartur's epic pride with both comedy and awe. Write what 'independence' costs the man who insists on it — and what it buys him.

name: Jón Kalman Stefánsson
teaser: The Icelandic novelist of sea, snow, and story — Summer Light, and Then Comes the Night and his trilogy about a boy who carries a book into the cold. His prose is both brutal and tender.

exploreAction.targetName: Summer Light, and Then Comes the Night, opening
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of the novel, which begins with a village and its restless residents. Notice how Stefánsson moves between voices and moods like weather. Write how the small town becomes a whole cosmos of longing.

name: Peter Høeg
teaser: The Danish novelist of Smilla's Sense of Snow — an arctic thriller about a woman who knows snow the way others know faces, and uses that knowledge to solve a murder the authorities would rather bury.

exploreAction.targetName: Smilla's Sense of Snow, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Smilla's Sense of Snow. Notice how Smilla's expertise — snow, ice, footprints — becomes the engine of the plot. Write how a special form of attention becomes both identity and method of truth.

name: Sigrid Combüchen
teaser: The Swedish-German novelist and essayist whose books — like The White Lie and About Beauty — are intricate, witty examinations of art, biography, and how stories get told and mistold.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The White Lie. Notice how Combüchen frames her narrator's unreliable memory as the subject itself. Write how the novel questions what we allow ourselves to believe about our own lives and art.

name: Lars Saabye Christensen
teaser: The Norwegian novelist of The Half Brother — a sprawling, funny, painful family saga set in Oslo after the war. His Beatles follows four boys growing up with the band and a changing Norway.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Beatles. Notice how Christensen catches the texture of a 1960s Oslo childhood — music, nicknames, small rebellions. Write how a pop band becomes the soundtrack and measure of growing up.

name: Jonas Lie
teaser: One of the four great figures of 19th-century Norwegian literature, alongside Ibsen, Bjørnson, and Kielland. His novels of seafaring families, like The Pilot and His Wife, made the coastal world feel mythic.

exploreAction.targetName: The Pilot and His Wife, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Pilot and His Wife. Notice how Lie makes the sea, the fjord, and the ship feel like extensions of his characters' inner lives. Write how the coastal setting shapes ambition and love in the novel.

name: Jens Peter Jacobsen
teaser: The Danish novelist and poet whose Niels Lyhne was a Bible for the European fin-de-siècle — a portrait of an atheist, a dreamer, and a failure that Rilke and others could not stop reading.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Niels Lyhne. Notice how Jacobsen's prose is lyrical and precise at once, and how his hero drifts between aspiration and passivity. Write how the novel made 'a life without illusions' feel both noble and sad.

name: Vilhelm Moberg
teaser: The Swedish novelist of The Emigrants series — the four-volume epic of a family leaving Småland for America in the 1850s. A people's history of emigration, written with immense warmth and plain grandeur.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Emigrants. Notice how Moberg grounds the decision to leave in the soil, the harvest, and the potato patch. Write how the novel makes you feel both the weight of home and the terror of departure.

name: Inger Edelfeldt
teaser: The Swedish novelist and translator, a boundary-crossing figure of Nordic letters whose fiction and essays have probed identity, migration, and the art of living between cultures and languages.

exploreAction.targetName: Inger Edelfeldt, a short story or essay
exploreAction.instruction: Read one of Edelfeldt's shorter works. Notice how identity is never settled in her fiction. Write how living between languages or cultures shapes a writer's sense of self, and how her work makes that visible.

name: Lu Xun
teaser: The founding father of modern Chinese literature. His story Diary of a Madman and his essay on the 'iron house' diagnosed China's sickness with savage wit. Every Chinese writer since has had to answer him.

exploreAction.targetName: Diary of a Madman, the full story
exploreAction.instruction: Read Diary of a Madman. Notice how the narrator's paranoia gradually becomes the reader's clarity about a society that eats people metaphorically and literally. Write how the 'madman' is the sanest person in the story.

name: Mo Yan
teaser: The Chinese Nobel laureate whose novels — Red Sorghum, Life and Death Are Wearing Me Out — are sprawling, sensual, magical chronicles of rural China. His narrator famously declared, 'I have a true story to tell.'

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Red Sorghum. Notice how Mo Yan immerses the reader in the smell and heat of the sorghum fields and the violence of the war years. Write how sensory excess carries history and legend at once.

name: Yu Hua
teaser: The Chinese novelist of To Live — the devastating saga of a man who survives every loss history can throw at him. Also wrote the darkly comic Brothers. His prose is plain, brutal, and deeply tender.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of To Live. Notice how Fugui's fortunes fall with a gambler's inevitability. Write how Yu Hua makes one man's losses into a record of a century, and what 'to live' means in the book's final accounting.

name: Cao Xueqin
teaser: The 18th-century author of Dream of the Red Chamber, the great novel of Chinese literature — a family's grandeur and ruin, told through a boy's love, a girl's poetry, and the fall of a clan.

exploreAction.targetName: Dream of the Red Chamber, the opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of the novel, with its frame of stone and dream and the household of the Jia family. Notice how the mundane and the mythic interweave. Write why this book is called the Chinese 'great novel' and what it mourns.

name: Eileen Chang
teaser: The Chinese writer of 1940s Shanghai whose stories of love, betrayal, and survival are among the sharpest ever written about urban life. Love in a Fallen City and Lust, Caution earned her a devoted afterlife.

exploreAction.targetName: Love in a Fallen City, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Love in a Fallen City. Notice how Chang's prose is diamond-hard and wry, and how her lovers negotiate like businessmen. Write how the fall of Hong Kong becomes the story's strange happy ending.

name: Kenzaburō Ōe
teaser: The Japanese Nobel laureate who turned his family and his nation's trauma into fiction — A Personal Matter about a father of a disabled son, and The Silent Cry about a village's revolt. Fierce, guilt-ridden, humane.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of A Personal Matter. Notice how Ōe's protagonist tries to escape his new responsibility through a fantasy of flight. Write how the novel makes a private crisis inseparable from public history — Hiroshima, guilt, survival.

name: Ryūnosuke Akutagawa
teaser: The Japanese master of the short story — Rashomon and In a Grove (the basis of Kurosawa's film) probe truth, selfishness, and the masks people wear. He killed himself at 35, haunted by madness.

exploreAction.instruction: Read both stories. Notice how Akutagawa withholds a single truth and offers competing testimonies instead. Write how In a Grove questions whether any account — including our own — is ever simply true.

name: Osamu Dazai
teaser: The Japanese novelist of No Longer Human — a confessional masterpiece of alienation that became a bible for disaffected readers. Dazai's life of drinking and affairs shadowed his work, which keeps its terrible lucidity.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of No Longer Human, where the narrator recalls being a child who performed happiness. Notice how Dazai's confessions feel both sincere and staged. Write how the book's title names a specific kind of exile.

name: Natsume Sōseki
teaser: The giant of modern Japanese literature — I Am a Cat, Kokoro, and Botchan balance comedy and loneliness. He watched Japan modernize and worried about what the West was doing to its soul.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Kokoro. Notice how the narrator's relationship with Sensei is built from reticence and hints. Write how Sōseki's novel of a secret guilt explores the gap between the modern and the traditional self.

name: Shūsaku Endō
teaser: The Japanese Catholic novelist of Silence — a priest in 17th-century Japan who must choose between apostasy and martyrdom. Endō's questions about faith, weakness, and the face of God made him a world writer.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Silence. Notice how Endō builds the story from letters and travel into a landscape of fear. Write what the novel suggests about a God who seems silent in suffering, and whether weakness can be a form of faithfulness.

name: Keigo Higashino
teaser: The Japanese master of the puzzle mystery — The Devotion of Suspect X and Malice are emotional, ingeniously plotted novels that have sold in the millions. He turned the whodunit into the why-dunit.

exploreAction.targetName: The Devotion of Suspect X, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Devotion of Suspect X. Notice how the 'trick' is hidden in full view from the first chapter. Write how Higashino makes the reader care about the criminal's logic as much as the detective's.

name: Miyazawa Kenji
teaser: The Japanese poet and children's author of Night on the Galactic Railroad — a Buddhist, a farmer, and a visionary who saw the cosmos in a field of potatoes. His tales are strange, tender, and vast.

exploreAction.targetName: Night on the Galactic Railroad, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Night on the Galactic Railroad. Notice how the train journey blends astronomy, grief, and Buddhist ideas of sacrifice. Write what the journey's mysterious ending suggests about life, death, and true happiness.

name: Hwang Sok-yong
teaser: The South Korean novelist of The Guest and Familiar Things — a dissident who lived through dictatorship and prison, and whose fiction braids Korea's modern traumas with folk wisdom and fierce compassion.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Guest. Notice how Hwang's narrator returns to a divided Korea, carrying both memory and exorcism. Write how the novel treats war and ideology as kinds of possession that must be spoken out.

name: Cho Nam-joo
teaser: The South Korean novelist of Kim Jiyoung, Born 1982 — the quiet, devastating account of one ordinary woman's life that ignited a nationwide reckoning with everyday sexism and became a global phenomenon.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Kim Jiyoung, Born 1982. Notice how Cho narrates a life in neutral clinical prose, and how that tone itself becomes the indictment. Write how documenting the ordinary can expose systemic harm.

name: Ko Un
teaser: The South Korean poet who lived through war, the dictatorship years, and prison — and produced tens of thousands of poems, from the epic Ten Thousand Lives to searing political verse and Zen-flavored stillness.

exploreAction.targetName: Ko Un's poems, a small selection
exploreAction.instruction: Read a handful of Ko Un's short poems. Notice how the smallest image — a weed, a stone, a monk's bowl — carries enormous weight. Write how poetry can hold both political anger and quiet Buddhist attention at once.

name: Yi Mun-yol
teaser: The South Korean novelist of Our Twisted Hero and The Poet — books that dissect power, corruption, and the moral compromises of modern Korean history with chilly, elegant prose.

exploreAction.targetName: Our Twisted Hero, the full novella
exploreAction.instruction: Read Our Twisted Hero. Notice how the classroom tyranny of the student boss mirrors larger systems of power. Write how Yi makes a schoolroom a parable of dictatorship — and how the twist complicates simple judgments.

name: Munshi Premchand
teaser: The giant of Hindi and Urdu fiction — Godan (The Gift of a Cow) follows a peasant's impossible struggle for a cow and dignity. He wrote the stories of India's poor with unsentimental compassion.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Godan. Notice how Premchand renders village economics — debt, caste, weather — with exactness. Write how Hori's longing for a cow becomes a measure of dignity, and what the novel says about debt's grip.

name: Saadat Hasan Manto
teaser: The Urdu writer of Partition who refused to look away — Toba Tek Singh and Cold Meat are explosive stories about madness, borders, and the body. He was tried for obscenity six times; he never stopped writing.

exploreAction.targetName: Toba Tek Singh, the full story
exploreAction.instruction: Read Toba Tek Singh, set in an asylum being divided between India and Pakistan. Notice how the inmates' confusion mirrors the nations' logic. Write how Manto uses absurdity to indict the border itself — and who 'the sane' really are.

name: Cao Yu
teaser: China's greatest modern playwright — Thunderstorm, a family tragedy of secrets and class set in a suffocating mansion, is a landmark of Chinese theatre and still staged constantly.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the first act of Thunderstorm. Notice how Cao Yu sets the weather, the servants, and the hidden family ties in motion before the storm breaks. Write how the play uses class and secrecy to build toward catastrophe.

name: Hwang Jini
teaser: The legendary 16th-century Korean poet and gisaeng whose sijo verses are among the most loved in the language — poems of love, wit, and freedom composed at the edge of a strict Confucian world.

exploreAction.instruction: Read a selection of Hwang Jini's sijo. Notice how each three-line verse turns on a clever pivot — often at the reader's expense. Write what her poems reveal about wit as a form of freedom for a woman of her time.

name: Li Bai
teaser: China's most beloved poet — the Tang dynasty's drunken, wandering, moon-loving immortal. His poems of friendship, wine, and exile are memorized by every Chinese schoolchild and live on in the world's imagination.

exploreAction.targetName: Li Bai's poems, a small selection
exploreAction.instruction: Read a handful of Li Bai's poems, including Drinking Alone by Moonlight. Notice how his lines move with effortless lightness. Write what the poems' freedom and loneliness suggest about the figure of the wanderer-poet.

name: Du Fu
teaser: Li Bai's great friend and China's poet of history — Du Fu wrote through war, exile, and hunger, and his poetry became the conscience of the nation. His careful craftsmanship frames an enormous empathy.

exploreAction.targetName: Du Fu's poems, a small selection
exploreAction.instruction: Read three of Du Fu's poems, including one from the war years. Notice how precise observation and pity share the same line. Write how Du Fu's poetry differs from Li Bai's — where one flies, the other stays to record.

name: Choi Seung-ja
teaser: A pioneering South Korean poet whose frank, image-rich verse broke the decorum of Korean poetry in the 1980s — writing about the body, desire, and daily life with startling directness.

exploreAction.instruction: Read a few of Choi Seung-ja's poems. Notice how the domestic and the bodily enter the poem without apology. Write what her directness meant for a generation of Korean women readers and writers.

name: Juan Rulfo
teaser: The Mexican writer who published almost nothing — but Pedro Páramo and The Burning Plain changed world literature. A village where the dead speak, and prose as dry and haunted as the dust.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Pedro Páramo. Notice how the dead narrator and the living traveler blur, and how the village of Comala is described as heat and murmur. Write how Rulfo builds a landscape where the afterlife is just another room.

name: José Saramago
teaser: The Portuguese Nobel laureate who wrote without conventional punctuation — long rivers of speech that pull you under. Blindness and Baltasar and Blimunda explore civilization's skin-thin veneer with rage and tenderness.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Blindness. Notice how the white blindness spreads from one man to a city, and how Saramago's run-on prose mirrors contagion. Write what the novel says about the social contract when everyone loses sight.

name: Fernando Pessoa
teaser: The Portuguese poet who wrote as many selves — heteronyms with their own biographies and styles: the modernist Álvaro de Campos, the neoclassical Ricardo Reis, the humble Alberto Caeiro. The Book of Disquiet is his strange masterpiece.

exploreAction.targetName: The Book of Disquiet, a selection
exploreAction.instruction: Read a selection of fragments from The Book of Disquiet. Notice how Pessoa's assistant bookkeeper narrator dreams instead of acts. Write how writing as invented selves might be a way to live many lives — or none at all.

name: Jorge Amado
teaser: The Brazilian novelist of Bahia — Dona Flor and Her Two Husbands, Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon. He filled his pages with heat, humor, food, and the street wisdom of the poor. His books sold in the millions.

exploreAction.targetName: Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon. Notice how Amado makes the town of Ilhéus — its cacao, its customs, its gossip — the real main character. Write how food, scent, and weather carry the novel's sensuality.

name: Pablo Neruda
teaser: The Chilean Nobel laureate — poet of love sonnets, odes to onions and socks, and the epic Canto General about Latin America's earth and history. He made poetry democratic, sensual, and political.

exploreAction.targetName: Twenty Love Poems, a selection, and an Ode
exploreAction.instruction: Read a few love poems and one ode (try Ode to the Onion or Ode to My Socks). Notice how Neruda makes the humble object magnificent. Write how the odes find the sacred in the everyday, and why that is a political act too.

name: Octavio Paz
teaser: The Mexican Nobel laureate — poet and essayist whose The Labyrinth of Solitude dissected Mexican identity, and whose poems (Sunstone, Blanco) are among the century's most beautiful meditations on time and love.

exploreAction.instruction: Read Sunstone. Notice how the poem's circular form loops the same line back after 584 verses. Write how Paz's meditation on a single moment — a woman, a room, the Aztec calendar — expands into all of history.

name: Horacio Quiroga
teaser: The Uruguayan master of the jungle story — his Tales of Love, Madness and Death and Jungle Tales turn the Misiones wilderness into a place of terrifying beauty. His life was as violent as his fiction.

exploreAction.targetName: The Decapitated Chicken, and one jungle tale
exploreAction.instruction: Read The Decapitated Chicken. Notice how Quiroga builds horror out of domestic detail and heredity. Write how his stories use the natural world as both refuge and threat, and what the title story says about obsession.

name: Adolfo Bioy Casares
teaser: The Argentine novelist and Borges's closest collaborator — The Invention of Morel is a perfect little novel about love, islands, and a machine that replays the past. Borges called it flawless.

exploreAction.targetName: The Invention of Morel, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Invention of Morel. Notice how the castaway narrator's observations slowly decode the island's ghostly visitors. Write how the novel turns science fiction into a meditation on love and mortality.

name: José Donoso
teaser: The Chilean novelist of The Obscene Bird of Night — a labyrinthine, Gothic masterwork about an old woman, her monsters, and the house where servants mimic their masters. Latin America's strangest novel of power.

exploreAction.targetName: The Obscene Bird of Night, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Obscene Bird of Night. Notice how identity dissolves and multiplies, and how the house breathes. Write how Donoso uses the grotesque to explore the master-servant relationship at the heart of his society.

name: Silvina Ocampo
teaser: The Argentine short-story writer and poet — Borges and Bioy's collaborator, whose stories twist childhood, cruelty, and the fantastic into glittering, disturbing miniatures. Rediscovered as a hidden giant.

exploreAction.targetName: Silvina Ocampo, a handful of stories
exploreAction.instruction: Read two or three of Ocampo's short stories. Notice how her child narrators observe adult cruelty with unsettling calm. Write what her fiction suggests about innocence — is it ever really innocent, or just another mask?

name: Alejandra Pizarnik
teaser: The Argentine poet of darkness and desire — her short, intense poems face the night, the mirror, and silence without blinking. She died at 36, and her voice has only grown louder.

exploreAction.instruction: Read a handful of Pizarnik's poems. Notice how few words she needs to create a whole night. Write what her poetry says about the desire to be seen and the fear of being seen, and why that tension still resonates.

name: Federico García Lorca
teaser: The Andalusian poet and playwright — Blood Wedding, Yerma, and The House of Bernarda Alba turned Spanish rural tragedy into timeless theatre. He was murdered by Franco's men in 1936 at 38.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the first act of Blood Wedding. Notice how the knife, the moon, and the lullaby carry the coming violence. Write how Lorca blends folk poetry and tragedy, and what the play says about desire against the law of the family.

name: Javier Marías
teaser: The Spanish novelist of A Heart So White and All Souls — a master of the long, digressive, hypnotic sentence and of stories told through what people almost said. Also a sharp essayist and translator.

exploreAction.targetName: A Heart So White, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of A Heart So White, which begins with a woman's suicide during her honeymoon. Notice how Marías circles events without ever quite landing on them. Write how the withheld telling becomes its own kind of suspense.

name: Carmen Laforet
teaser: The Spanish novelist who, at 23, wrote Nada — a devastating portrait of postwar Barcelona and a girl's arrival into a house full of ghosts. It won the first Nadal Prize and changed Spanish fiction.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Nada. Notice how Andrea arrives in the dark city and the claustrophobic apartment. Write how Laforet makes hunger, poverty, and a family's decay feel like weather pressing on one girl.

name: Arturo Pérez-Reverte
teaser: The Spanish novelist of The Club Dumas and the Captain Alatriste series — swashbuckling, erudite, and dark. A former war correspondent, he writes about honor, books, and the sea with equal passion.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Club Dumas. Notice how Pérez-Reverte treats rare books as objects of obsession and danger. Write how the novel blends detective story, book history, and the occult into a single page-turning engine.

name: Carlos Ruiz Zafón
teaser: The Spanish author of The Shadow of the Wind — a love letter to Barcelona and to books, set in a Cemetery of Forgotten Books. It became one of the best-selling Spanish novels ever written.

exploreAction.targetName: The Shadow of the Wind, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Shadow of the Wind. Notice how the Cemetery of Forgotten Books is described as a holy place for readers. Write how the novel makes the act of choosing a book — and losing one — into a mystery.

name: Rosa Montero
teaser: The Spanish novelist and journalist whose fiction — The Lunatic of the House, Weep, My Lady — braids journalism, fantasy, and autobiography into a search for how stories keep us alive.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lunatic of the House, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Lunatic of the House. Notice how Montero's narrator invents an alter ego to explore her own fears and desires. Write how the novel uses fantasy as a tool for honesty rather than escape.

name: Rosa Chacel
teaser: The Spanish novelist in the line of the great modernists — her dense, introspective fiction, like The Maravillas District, explores memory and the female self. She spent decades of exile in Brazil.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Maravillas District. Notice how Chacel's prose moves by association, circling memory rather than narrating it. Write how her experimental style gives access to an inner life that traditional realism flattens.

name: Rosario Castellanos
teaser: The Mexican writer and diplomat who wrote about women and indigenous life with irony and fury — The Book of Lamentations and her poems are essential reading for understanding Mexico's inner fractures.

exploreAction.targetName: The Book of Lamentations, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Book of Lamentations. Notice how Castellanos gives voice to a Tzotzil woman's rebellion against both church and state. Write how the novel weaves colonial history into one woman's fierce refusal.

name: Elena Poniatowska
teaser: The Polish-born Mexican journalist and novelist of The Night of Tlatelolco — the oral history of the 1968 massacre that made her Mexico's conscience. Also wrote the dazzling biography Dear Diego.

exploreAction.targetName: The Night of Tlatelolco, opening sections
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Night of Tlatelolco. Notice how Poniatowska stitches together testimonies, slogans, and official lies. Write how oral history as a literary form can do what official accounts refuse to.

name: Rosa Regàs
teaser: The Spanish novelist and publisher — a free spirit of the Barcelona literary scene whose novels like Azul explore passion, memory, and the life of a woman who refuses the roles handed to her.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Azul. Notice how Regàs weaves present and past, and how the sea functions as both setting and memory. Write how the novel uses recollection to measure what a woman's freedom has cost her.
